My original plan was to get well into the game before I did a review. I've  got over 50 hours in at this point and I am just leaving the first sector LOL.  This game is so damn good. I have no idea why the reviews are mixed.  If you like strategy and space games just get this one.  I've paid more than twice the cost of this game for some big name titles  and not gotten nearly as much enjoyment.

Get a ship, assemble a crew, get missions, keep flying.  There is a LOT more to it than this but if there wasn't it would be totally worth your $25.

One perk that I have immensely enjoyed has been the ability to import custom portraits for your characters.  With the included portraits, some photos from friends and family and a little help from ChatGPT they have flying the stars and hitting the ground on away missions with me :D. Some of you may remember the ability to do this from Baldur's Gate II except it is FAR easier. No resizing necessary. 

If you decide to get this game (and you should) my advice would be to give it a little time.  The learning curve can be a little inconsistent in that you get hand holding and tutorials with some things and not with others. There is a good guide within the game that you can access at any time. For me, I get a great amount of joy when I discover something for myself.  There have been many utterances of "Ohhhhh"  "Ahhhhh now I see"  The figuring it out could be frustrating for some and rewarding for others.

Of Note: I purchased the game sometime last year I think when it was on sale but was waiting until release to actually play it. After purchase I had installed the game and then ran updates as they became available. After playing for a few hours I started getting game freezes.  I did the normal video driver update and then file verification but the problem continued.  I finally completely uninstalled the game and reinstalled it fresh and I have not had any issues whatsoever. My saved games were good to go so no restarts necessary. 

This game is a lot of bang for your buck and super fun.

Being a one man project earns some understanding, but not quite forgiveness. 

It's impressive how much was accomplished by a single person's vision, and tons of store assets. And the scope of the universe is very impressive. Bonus points for allowing custom portraits, and sliders to customize the experience!
But that starts to falter when, 130 hours in, I've only seen three types of dungeons with the same six kinds of rooms. 
And the absolute grind- I felt I didn't start to get decent gear until about 80 hours in, and a nice ship at around 100 hours. 
Couple that with pretty bad combat glitches of being shot through a doorframe, or a rocket round going through what I thought was a solid window (that it still wouldn't let me shoot out of) hitting my whole squad. 
There's narrative issue too- where it sets you up for some interesting things, but the way events turn out leaves you like you were overthinking it. 

I mean no disrespect to the developer, but my review is kind of a mess. And so is this game.

*** Recommended, if you're in for a long haul game. 

It's basically EvE Offline + Simplified XCom. Which to me is awesome, but it requires a time and brain investment. It really scratches the space game itch for me, and the ground gameplay can be fun, or kinda frustrating and excessive at times. It's good to note that there's MULTIPLE difficulty sliders for this game to help fine-tune your experience. If you don't like the ground combat, for example, there's a specific slider to turn that down to easy.

It's also helpful to note that apparently you can skip at least the first of TWO "tutorial" story dungeons before you even get your ship. I played through them but found them kinda excessive for a game intro, as did many others who have left reviews. 

I did, however, arrive at a very satisfying gameloop so far, and I haven't even left the home star system yet.

1. Start as Explorer
2. Slog through both tutorial/intro dungeons, somehow.
3. Ditch the 2 creepy crewmembers you start with...well, one super creepo and one who's stockholm syndromed to the creepo. 
4. Hire some decent folks at the first station.
5. Sell off gear I don't need to buy a HEAVY Mining Laser for the starter Explorer ship.
6. Start mining/selling.
7. Find shipwreck close to main trade station.
8. Realize I now have access to infinite AFK money over time.
9. Upgrade WARP DRIVE among other components, as energy output seems to be the main reason you can't fight anything in the starter Explorer.
10. Explode my first rat, find Exceptional Ore Refinery. Jackpot. More money, can refine on the go for bigger hauls. (And you can hot swap your ship gear while in space!)

The game has a lot to enjoy, if you're into the sandbox, grindy, numbers-go-up, space game experience. For me, so far it's what I've been looking for in a space game for a long time. There's a lot of gear, lots of things to level up, and lots of ways to play and make money. Plus, I guess there's some story in there about a threat to the whole galaxy yada yada...

Recommended, to a playerbase that appreciates this type of game.

PROS
~~~~~
- Ground combat is well balanced and fun
- Hacking, Crafting, Repairing, and Salvaging are worth the time investment
- The many methods of Fast Travel respects the players time (FTL Button, Beacons, Warp Gates, Sector Fast Travel Button)
- The economy is balanced and always has something to work towards
- Shops are usually worth visiting to try and find Legendary items.  

CONS
~~~~~
- The Cave maps are far too LARGE for how often you are sent to them. 
- "Kill High Value Target" is the only mission type that's worth the time investment (kill boss and leave.)
- Space Combat skills level up far too slow (Intelligence does nothing and the +20% in the Gameplay Options is not enough.)
- Reputation levels up far too slow (I shouldnt be Neutral with a Faction after 50 extremely long missions.)
- Psionics makes the First Aid skill useless
- F5 and F9 let you Quick Save and Quick Load but the Control Menu doesn't mention this.
- Autosaves should be after X number of minutes (you can lose hours of mining / ship combat progress)

BUGS
~~~~~
- New characters that you hire can sometimes be invisible or "off the map" requiring a Reload to change zones.
- Pugilism weapons don't appear on character models but do appear on enemy models.
- Sometimes the game crashes if you enter FTL at the same time you try to use a Beacon.
- Enemies can sometimes become untargetable due to the mouse cursor being stuck in movement mode.

Stellar Tactics is one of those rare indie RPGs that quietly delivers more content, freedom, and depth than most big‑studio releases and for it's low purchase price, it’s honestly a steal.

This is a massive, open‑ended sci‑fi universe built by a single developer, and the amount of work, care, and long‑term dedication behind it really shows. Knowing the dev pushed through personal hardship to keep this project alive only makes the achievement more impressive.

There is a full sci‑fi storyline here involving the Phage and it’s genuinely interesting, but what I love is that the game never forces you down that path. You can follow the narrative when you feel like it, or you can just as easily carve out your own path exploring the galaxy.

If you enjoy turn‑based combat, ship‑to‑ship battles, boarding actions, exploration, and building your own story at your own pace, this game absolutely delivers. The universe is huge — genuinely huge — and wandering through it, taking contracts, upgrading your ship, and shaping your squad feels incredibly rewarding. The game fully supports running multiple ships for different roles. I like that you can have one dedicated to exploration, another for mining, and a third built purely for ship‑to‑ship combat, and swapping between them is smooth.

Sure, there are places that could use more polish, but the core experience is rock solid, and I haven’t run into any issues or crashes while playing. The combat is fun, the progression is deep, and the freedom to play your way is exactly what a sandbox RPG should offer.

For the price, the scope, and the sheer ambition of a one‑person project, Stellar Tactics deserves far more love. If you’re even remotely into sci‑fi RPGs or tactical combat, give it a try, there’s a genuinely great game here.

In my opinion this game is not polished enough to be called a 1.0 release

2. If I understand correctly, this game has fog of war when detecting enemies. There does not seem to be much of a way to control what direction your characters look in, or how they patrol. There does not seem to be an option to enable normal fog of war so you can see what areas of the map your characters can see - as a result, enemies will seem to appear out of thin air from an area that a character could have readily shot at. I have not found any way to disable this.

3. I've encountered a bug where when these invisible enemies block pathfinding, the AP cost estimate does not reflect this, and your character *will* spend their entire turn running off in some random direction instead of doing what seemed like a 1 ap step.

These problems are just kind of stupid ones to have in a full release, so I can't recommend the game.

A huge galaxy with lots to do.  By huge I mean your great grandchildren's great grandchildren will finally finish the game for you when they clear the scavver base on the 600,000th planet in the game.  You can do quests from faction agents or other faction npcs for reputation and rewards, do urgent cargo pickup and delivery missions for financial payout, do ship parts acquisition (boarding) missions, defeat phage, mutant, scavver, or other attacks that you stumble across while exploring, do your own thing trading using the trade-net network that you create by deploying beacons, or simply roam around exploring stars, scanning planets, and deploying mining drones.  Money (credits) is pretty easy to come by -- I came out of the tutorial (Dauntless) with about 60,000 credits if I remember right and most missions involving ground combat will give 50,000 or so between rewards and loot.  Faction agents will pay well for your planet scans.  Once you buy and deploy your first Mining Drone you are pretty well set financially -- keep buying drones until you reach your limit of 20 and you will have a strong, steady income.  After 60 hours spent mostly exploring/scanning, managing mining drones, and a dozen or so ground missions I have my initial explorer ship mostly upgraded to Exceptional components with 6.6 million credits saved up towards getting a strong combat ship, which will cost about 20 million credits to start.

Ground combat with your 4 person away team is satisfying if not as thorough as some other games; for example there's not much opportunities for use of cover, it's not clear if partial cover is a thing, and you can't go prone.  One of the most important things for ground combat is having plenty of stun grenades and using them without hesitation.  Get in the habit of checking the merchant and weapons merchants for stun and frag grenades every time you stop in an orbital station or starport.

Characters get 5 attribute points to spend every level.  Weapon and non-combat skills improve only by using them.  Characters have a primary and secondary weapon slot and they can freely switch between them without Action Point cost, whereas swapping in a weapon from inventory costs 4 AP.  The type of weapon determines which slot it can go into -- rifles, shotguns, big guns, 2 hand melee can only go into the primary weapon slot for example while pistols, SMGs, 1 hand melee, and pugilism can only go into the secondary weapon slot.  This makes some equipped combinations impossible, like you can't have your rifle and 2 hand melee weapon equipped at the same time, but you can swap in the other during combat for 4 AP if you really want to.  I have not yet found the perfect combination of weapon skills which is probably a good thing.  From what I've seen, the mercenaries you can recruit have a limited selection of weapon skills like rifle/pistol, shotgun/smg, big guns/pugilism, 2 hand melee/1 hand melee.  Rifles and some of the big guns (orion fusion gun and missile launchers) have the best range so everyone should probably have some skill in either of those.

Having explored most of the stars in the sectors immediately surrounding the one I started in, I've found ship combat to be completely avoidable which is a relief since I started with the explorer ship.  When I buy my 18 million credit heavy attack ship I will perhaps try ship combat against a vastly weaker opponent.  So far I'm enjoying the exploration and ground combat enough that I don't feel the lack of ship combat.

I don't have anything negative to say about the gameplay although I imagine at some point it may start to feel repetitive.  The backstory on the other hand is fairly ludicrous -- as Earth was being destroyed by an asteroid humanity assembled starships designed to last longer than human history, which apparently was easier than just deflecting the asteroid a few degrees while it was a few million miles away.  Not to mention what are essentially space zombies.  So we get some chuckles out of the plot but that doesn't harm the gameplay.  The graphics in space are beautiful but the orbitals and bases all have the same look, including the Kchor (which I assume are aliens although all their npcs are humanoid).  Also the narrator gal seems to say "FDL [sic] drive disengaged" instead of "FTL".  But again that doesn't affect the fun gameplay.

It's a great game for only $20.

Ignore my playtime, I had a kip and left the PC on, so at the time of this review. I probably had about 4 hours at review time.

I would recommend visiting the technical help on the Steam discussions before starting the game (I had a CTD afrer an hour, losing 30 mins of play - voting it down before deciding to give it another try. Since tweaking everything seems to be running smoothly. Secondly the in-game tutorials aren't great and it's worth pressing the 'H' key and browsing through the comprehensive play guide. 'F5' is quicksave (as you would expect) although I didn't see this flagged in-game.

It's difficult to criticise the ambition and sheer scope at this price point. But there is a trade off in the depth of the mechanics. The idea of leading a space mercenary group going gung-ho round a dynamic open universe really does appeal. Battle Brothers/ Wartales in space? I'm sold! Ignore the main quest and go off and do your own thing? Sign me up! There's plenty of stats, perks and skills to keep the RPG aficionado's happy - although irritatingly you don't retain your companions in the opening part of the game. 

From what I've seen of the ground combat - it's decent enough, but not particularly deep. There is a cover system (apparently) but it completely passed me by in the opening sections. I miss overwatch - which I feel is a necessity in any tactics based RPG. Be warned, there's also RNG to hit, and the fixed isometric camera can feel restrictive. Yes you can rotate and zoom..... but I found myself really wanting to tilt it! Maps are of the 'boxy' design - for the procedural generation I assume, and the graphics are decent enough. I can see this feeling repetitive after a while - and to make it bearable my advice is to stock up on grenades. Lots of them. Attacking my first base, it's difficult not to feel nostalgia for that "Aliens" vibe, sweeping through rooms and taking out mutants. 

Some minor QOL issues. I'm still looking for the filter key that allows me to only bring up selected items in my inventory and occasionally things seem very... illogical. (Minor spoiler: Why does killing a thing magically open a door?).  Needs a loot all button (and a repair all for that matter) and an exit-mission button, without the in-game mcguffin of a thing which needs another thing to power it.  What is a nice touch is the variability of difficulty - you get to tweak the game to how you want on a variety of options. Good call there.

The space flight is good, with a whopping great universe to explore - it does tickle that Freelancer itch. BUT it desperately needs a fixed camera. I found movement of the ship with a free camera which I can't lock difficult to work when taking on a bad guy. My first combat encounter felt incredibly clunky (just one enemy, I dread to think how awkward this would be with multiple enemies). The game is much stronger on the tactical turn based ground combat. 

The joy of games like this, is that they allow you to make your own fun. For that degree of freedom in a sci-fi setting, this sparks a win for me,  Just be aware that the presentation won't blow you away and the mechanics may feel limiting. On the flip side at this price point for what the title offers it is worth taking a punt.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
+ I've played a lot of CRPGs and I swear the to-hit chance is rigged or not accurate to the numbers. I can't tell you how many times in Fallout and such I would miss 95% chance to hit twice in a row. Meanwhile landing a 10% chance to hit seems impossible and I fail 20 times in a row (not hyperbole). 50% chance might as well be about 33%. However this is the first game where the to-hit chance seems accurate. You will rarely miss and it feels good. I think part of it is that for certain (if not all) weapons if you make a low roll then rather than missing you deal less damage. The big guns beam weapon for instance never appears to miss, but it seems like you do less damage the lower your to-hit chance. Special attacks don't ever seem to miss.
+ I like the concept of ground based CRPG gameplay while being able to fly around in your ship and fight other ships.
+ Tons of loot, though it can get tedious dealing with it all.
+ Gameplay options that let you customize your experience such as making the game easy or harder for both ground and space battles, earn more or less experience, buy and sell items for more or less, and some others.
+ Your skills level up based on use, which I'm always a fan of.
+ Grenades, mainly stun, are OP. Use them. Any character has perfect aim with them at any skill level and the range you can throw is huge.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
- My biggest problem that hampers my enjoyment are the real long load times, even on an SSD and hardware way above requirements. The preload when you boot up the game is fine, but even with that transitioning between areas still takes 10-30 seconds. And there's a lot of transitions. Finish a mission on a planet then teleport to ship > teleport to FTL space > teleport closer to next system > enter system > fly then land on next planet. Where each > is a transition taking 10-30 seconds each. So much time spent just getting around. If the game was fast with 2 second loads tops it would be a massive improvement.
- The above is compounded by the fact the gameplay itself is slow. I get there aren't many fast paced CRPGs, it's an inherently slow system, but it's also the tedium of item management from the tons of loot you get (and you need loot to buy ships). I suppose though you could ignore all loot except the valuable epic and legendary. However you still need to salvage stuff for parts to repair your gear and to earn schematics to craft. I also suppose you can turn off gear wear and just not worry about crafting, though I think the best gear is only craftable.
- The third major problem is that because everything is procedurally generated it becomes extremely repetitive very fast. You will be fighting the same enemies in the same rooms you've seen a bunch of times already. Only the main mission is unique. So I would actually recommend ignoring the randomly generated quests and just focus on the main story as much as you can so you don't get burnt out fast like I did.
- There's still a bunch of bugs but I'm sure the dev will fix most of them in future patches.
- How this game implements line of sight is stupid. You can only see enemies if one of your characters is facing them. This means enemies can literally disappear from your view, including in the middle of combat. I get them running around a corner and then you can't see them, but they can still disappear out in the open if no one happens to be facing that way. Very annoying, unintuitive, and not challenging.
- A lot of stuff isn't explained to the player and you just have to figure it out. Like different weapons give you different movement speeds. For example you move slow with big guns, so just switch to your secondary before you move. Why program this? Adds more tedium and no challenge, to waste time switching to your secondary just to move so you can then switch back to your main weapon.
- Ship combat was confusing for me but I only tried it a few times and very quickly died. Don't try ship combat until you've beefed up your ship or you'll just lose.
- There just doesn't seem to be much variance in what you do in the game, building off the repetitive aspect.
- Mining is extremely slow. This isn't an MMO, you don't have to make it take forever to mine stuff in your ship.
- UI takes some getting used to, and some of the text is real tiny (so I imagine unplayable on Steamdeck even if it worked). The reputation window is currently unreadable even at 1080p on a monitor, hopefully he fixes it.

I'm still giving a thumbs up because while this isn't my cup of tea in the long run due to the first 3 negative points I make, but if those don't bother you then this is still a fine game. However I'd recommend a sale.

Tip: turn your experience gain to max (you will still level very slow), and reduce the cost of ships and increase the cost of items you sell. This will help a bit with the grind to get better ships, and isn't cheating because it still takes forever.

This game is fantastic, and that's coming from someone who has owned this game for years on Early Access, kept checking back after updates, and has restarted the campaign multiple times to ensure I was enjoying the most up-to-date features, fixes, and functions. I know that a lot of people will say this is an amazing game simply due to the fact that it was all designed and programmed by a single developer, and while that is quite a damn impressive feat — that's not the reason it's amazing. It's an amazing game due to the fact that it has a wealth of features, a semi-decent story (the writing isn't stellar, but that's alright), multiple, fleshed-out gameplay loops such as turn-based tactical combat, real-time ship-to-ship combat, exploration, trade, and much more — and it does each of those things pretty darn well. 

The amount of loot you collect is astonishing, and each weapon has more than enough attributes to give even clearly-randomized weapons of the same type / model some substantial differences. I think the attribute system leaves a little to be desired, but the skills are a fantastic split between combat, world engagement, and ship roles. Not to mention, any squad member can level any of the skills and they are increased purely through use - all the way up to level 100 - each of those levels coming with a unique perk attached to it which is directly associated with its base skill.

Performance-wise this game can conceivably be handled by pretty old hardware given its relatively low graphical demand, and the settings can be tweaked accordingly. I've attached my PC specs and can obviously max the settings on this game, but I've also played it while in EA on a slightly older gaming laptop and still got away with max settings at 1440p or even 4K (though it did have a Ryzen 9 and an GeForce G/RTX 3080).

There are a lot of games I've been playing over the past couple of years while owning Stellar Tactics and have enjoyed / am enjoying to varying degrees including Cyberpunk 2077, Baldur's Gate III, Starfield, Crimson Desert, an Avowed run (which I may or may not have abandoned), Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, The Alters, Battletech, Everspace 2, and many others — but all the while I keep coming back for more with Stellar Tactics.

Furthermore, I've rarely seen indie games with such levels of polish. You'll be able to obviously tell that it wasn't released by a AAA studio, but it performs damn well and is packed with a hell of a lot of content for an indie title - let along a single person. I'd dare say it has vastly more content than some of those AAA releases (it certainly performs better in many cases).

Like I said — I've owned this game for some time now in EA and am very excited to see the 1.0 release. I actually stumbled upon it after forcing it to update so I could play it instead of Crimson Desert this afternoon. This game is worth far, far more than the $17.99 sale price at the time of writing — and you can be absolutely certain you'll be getting your money's worth with this title.
